name: Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness

info.desc: Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness is the third album by American alternative rock band The Smashing Pumpkins, released on October 24, 1995 on Virgin Records. Produced by Smashing Pumpkins frontman Billy Corgan, Flood and Alan Moulder, the 28-track album was released as a two-disc CD and triple LP. Flood and Moulder had previously worked with Nine Inch Nails to produce 1994's The Downward Spiral. Led by the single "Bullet with Butterfly Wings", the album debuted at number one on the Billboard charts, a first for the group. The album spawned four more singles over the course of 1996 and .

podcast.body: Mark Ellis (Flood) instructed Billy Corgan to significantly increase their recording resources for the complex multi-track process they desired. This involved using multiple recording rooms simultaneously, allowing for separate tracking of elements like Billy Corgan's vocals and James Iha's guitar arrangements. Furthermore, even within a single song, guitar tracks had to be subdivided into multiple sub-tracks for meticulous layering and differentiation. "necesitaban varias salas de grabación al mismo tiempo, donde una persona pudiese estar ganando la voz de Bili Corgan mientras al Jens Hyatt, por ejemplo, podía estar ganando a arreglar los editarra y, sobre todo, incluso las pistas de editarra dentro de una misma canción tenían que serán subes divididas en pistas de las pistas de editarra dentro de la misma canción."

podcast.body: One of the first three albums that established the "defining smashing pumpkin sound" characterized by "big guitars, loud soft dynamics, great drumming, and Billy Corgan's whisper to a wine to his scream vocals." "Those first three albums, Gish, Simea's Dream, and Melon Cully and the Infinite Sadness, found what became the defining smashing pumpkin sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Released in 1995, this double album was conceived as a concept record despite the mid-90s stigma against such ambitious projects, which were considered egotistical and "dumb" by the Alternative Nation. Billy Corgan insisted on creating what he called "The Wall for Generation X," referencing Pink Floyd's iconic album. With producers Alan Molder and Flood, the band created a thematically unified album (though without a linear narrative) exploring the cycle of life and death. Corgan intended it as a message and an exploration of his own experiences, advice, and observations for Generation X, specifically those between entering high school and graduating college. The CD version was divided into "Dawn to Dusk" and "Twilight to Starlight," while the vinyl offered more granular sections: "Dawn," "Tea Time," "Dusk," "Twilight," "Midnight," and "Starlight." "Billy Corgan says that it was definitely conceived as a concept record."

podcast.body: Thanks to the intervention of Mark Ellis (Flood), the recording of "Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness" became much more democratic. James Iha had significant input into guitar arrangements and even had a song composed by him included on the album. Other band members also contributed ideas to the production work, even if not officially credited as producers. "Marquelys, que hizo mucho desicólogo dentro de la grabación, fue una persona que intervino mucho para ayudar a que la grabación del Melon Collir fue mucho más democrática."

"During the World Tour for the Melancholy and the Infinite Sadness Album in 1996, the group stopped at the point theater in Dublin, Ireland on May 11."

podcast.body: The recording of this album marked the beginning of the real classic dissolution of the band. Billy Corgan reportedly recorded almost all the solos and instruments. James Iha had composed several songs that Billy Corgan removed from the setlist to only include his own, though some of Iha's compositions eventually appeared. This period saw the band almost break up for the first time, marking the beginning of an emotional decline within the group. "cuando Billikon había grabado prácticamente el solo en melón Coli todos los instrumentos como James Saiya había compuesto varias canciones que Billikon había retirado del set list de la del melón Coli para poner solo canciones suyas aunque bueno acaba acaba apareciendo alguna cosa y la perdida de James Saiya y decía que ella la banda por primera vez había estado a punto de romperse y que había sido el principio del fin."

podcast.body: This "Magnum Opus" was a multi-platinum album and strong competition for Album of the Year at the 1997 Grammys. It was described as sounding more like the mid-90s than Celine Dion's "Falling Into You," which controversially won the award. podcast.body: This album is cited as a notable instance, similar to Tool's Lateralus, where technical constraints led to discrepancies in track order between different physical formats. Specifically, the intended tracklist designed for the compact disc version could not be fully accommodated on vinyl records due to limitations on the maximum length of audio per side, necessitating a rearrangement of songs for the vinyl release. "Como nos pasó muchos discos, como el melo en colide, los es más sin pánquiz, que bueno, tu en una cara del disco podés poner una longitud máxima de sonido y no cabían las canciones en el orden en el que las habían pensado para el disco compacto dentro de los discos de vinilo."

This album is considered a key piece for understanding 90s music in the United States. For its production, the band decided to replace their previous producer, Butch Vig, with two European producers, Alan Moulder and Flood (Mark Ellis), which was a significant risk and a major change for the album. The European producers revolutionized the recording process, making the band start from scratch due to fundamental differences in production techniques between Europe and the United States in the 90s. Mark Ellis advised the band to abandon their previous process, focusing instead on a more track-divided recording approach that prioritized well-recorded individual tracks. He also suggested dedicating a couple of hours daily to improvisation, creating new material without sheet music, which directly led to the creation of significant instrumental pieces like the album's title track. Alan Moulder, from day one, challenged Billy Corgan to define a guiding theme or narrative for the album, an idea that deeply resonated with Corgan but was complex given that most of the album was already composed. This pursuit of a conceptual thread led them to change some songs and discard over half of the existing material. The chosen theme for the album became "the sadness and personal frustration a person suffers throughout their life." The final guitar arrangements, especially the use of pedals and echo effects, aligned much more with 90s European rock production styles than with those prevalent in the US, a direction Billy Corgan greatly appreciated. "el meloncoli de los esmas simpánquis es una pizza clave para entender la música que se hizo en los 90 dentro de los Estados Unidos."

podcast.body: This album was a successful "sprawling album" by the Smashing Pumpkins, which their record company referenced when advising against another similar-length record for their fifth album. "It was like, look guys, you did find with Melon Colley in the Infinite Sadness, so take your weddings and just run."

podcast.body: This double album saw significant global success, reaching number one on charts in Canada, the US, Australia, New Zealand, and Sweden, and charting in the top 10 in many other countries. With total sales of around 10 million copies, the album's success was greatly aided by the critically acclaimed and expensive music video for one of its five singles, "Tonight, Tonight." "Not only did the video win a bunch of awards, but it helped Melancholy, a double album, reached number one on many of the charts around the world, including Canada, the US, Australia, New Zealand, and Sweden."
